summary: This standards-track RFC adds an optional extension to the Two-Way Active Measurement Protocol, allowing the TWAMP-Test protocol to monitor the Differentiated Services Code Point and Explicit Congestion Notification fields of test packets. It updates RFC 5357.

eli5.summary: When measuring how packets travel, this lets you also check the priority stickers and the traffic jam warnings on each packet.

questions: what is dscp and ecn monitoring in twamp
which twamp modes bit is dscp and ecn monitoring
subtitle: An optional TWAMP extension that lets the reflector report which DSCP and ECN values its test packets arrived with.

tldr.problem: TWAMP requires the same DSCP value to be used in both directions, but the test protocol has no way to find out when that value was changed along the path, or whether ECN congestion was signalled.
tldr.mechanism: A new flag (bit position 8) in the TWAMP Modes field lets Server and Control-Client agree to a changed Session-Reflector packet that carries a Sender DSCP and ECN (S-DSCP-ECN) field copied from the received test packet.
tldr.outcome: The Session-Sender can see the DSCP and ECN values that actually reached the reflector. The RFC is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 5357.

today: RFC 7750 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 5357. No later RFC obsoletes it, so it remains the definition of DSCP and ECN monitoring in TWAMP.

sections.title: The Problem: Silent DSCP Changes
sections.content:
The Two-Way Active Measurement Protocol (TWAMP, RFC 5357) measures network performance by sending test packets between a Session-Sender and a Session-Reflector. It says that only a Differentiated Services Code Point (DSCP) value can be defined by the Type-P Descriptor, and that the same DSCP value found in the Session-Sender packet MUST be used in the reflected test packet.

What TWAMP-Test does not do is say how to detect or report that the DSCP value has changed, or differs from what was expected, in the forward or reverse direction. Re-marking the DSCP is possible in IP networks and is often done by a Differentiated Services policy configured on a single node along the path. In many cases a change indicates unintentional or erroneous behavior. At best, the Session-Sender can detect a change in the reverse direction.

This RFC adds an OPTIONAL feature called DSCP and ECN Monitoring. It tells the Session-Sender the DSCP value actually received at the Session-Reflector, and also tracks the Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) value, which helps show whether ECN is operating or whether an ECN-capable node has detected congestion in the forward direction.
sections.eli5: Packets carry a priority sticker, and a router somewhere might swap it without telling anyone. This extension lets the receiver say what sticker it saw.

sections.title: Agreeing to Monitor During Setup
sections.content:
Connection setup follows RFC 4656 and RFC 5357, where the Modes field selects communication capabilities. The Modes field also works as an extension mechanism (RFC 6038), and this feature uses it: a new flag marks the ability of a Session-Reflector to return the received DSCP and ECN values and to use the new reflector packet format.

The Server sets the DSCP and ECN Monitoring flag in the Modes field of the Server Greeting to show that it can and is willing to monitor. If the Control-Client agrees to monitor DSCP and ECN on some or all test sessions of this control connection, it MUST set the same flag in the Modes field of the Setup Response message.
sections.eli5: Before the game starts, the receiver says it can report stickers, and the sender says yes please. Both have to agree first.

sections.title: The Sender DSCP and ECN Field
sections.content:
Monitoring needs support in the Session-Reflector and changes the reflected test packet format in all three original modes (unauthenticated, authenticated and encrypted). The Session-Sender test packet format is not altered.

The reflector builds a one-octet S-DSCP-ECN field for each packet it sends back. The six least-significant bits of the Differentiated Service field of the received packet MUST be copied into the Sender DSCP (S-DSCP) part, and the two ECN bits MUST be copied into the Sender ECN (S-ECN) part.

In the reflected packet the field sits right after the Sender TTL octet. In unauthenticated mode the layout is Sequence Number, Timestamp, Error Estimate, MBZ, Receive Timestamp, Sender Sequence Number, Sender Timestamp, Sender Error Estimate, MBZ, then Sender TTL, S-DSCP-ECN and MBZ, followed by Packet Padding. Authenticated and encrypted modes use the same idea with more MBZ space and a 16-octet HMAC.
sections.eli5: The receiver copies the sticker's details onto a small note and tucks it into the reply, in a spot right next to the note about how many hops the packet had left.

sections.title: How the Reflector Behaves
sections.content:
The DSCP and ECN values (part of the Type-P Descriptor) can be provisioned through TWAMP-Control or by other means such as a command-line interface or a central controller. With this extension the Session-Reflector MUST extract the DSCP and ECN values from the received packet and MUST use them to populate the S-DSCP-ECN field of the reflected packet. It MUST transmit each reflected packet with the DSCP set to the provisioned value.

If the provisioned DSCP is not known (for example in TWAMP Light), the choice is implementation specific: the reflector MAY copy the DSCP from the received packet, or MAY set it to CS0 (zero). If the provisioned ECN value is not known, ECN SHOULD be set to the Not-ECT codepoint; otherwise the provisioned ECN value SHALL be used.

The reflector does not analyze or act on the ECN value of the received packet, so it ignores congestion indications from the network. The RFC expects sending rates to be low enough, based on TWAMP deployment experience since 2008, that this will not significantly add to congestion.
sections.eli5: The receiver writes down the sticker it saw, then sends its reply with the sticker it was told to use. It does not slow down just because the road looked busy, since these test packets are few.

sections.title: Combining With RFC 6038 Modes and TWAMP Light
sections.content:
RFC 6038 defined Symmetrical Size and Reflects Octets modes. If either is negotiated together with DSCP and ECN Monitoring in unauthenticated mode, the extra field makes the unauthenticated Session-Reflector packet 4 octets larger. The Padding Length value therefore SHOULD be greater than or equal to 28 octets, so the truncation that RFC 5357 recommends still works.

For TWAMP Light, Appendix I of RFC 5357 does not say how the Type-P Descriptor is synchronized between sender and reflector. This RFC assumes that both have been informed by some means, such as configuration, to use the same DSCP value. The same configuration could tell the reflector to support the monitoring mode by copying data from received packets, and tell the Session-Sender to use the S-DSCP-ECN field in reflected packets.
sections.eli5: If the reply gets a bit bigger because of the extra note, you need to leave a little more room in the envelope so everything still fits.

sections.title: The Registered Mode Bit
sections.content: In the TWAMP-Modes registry defined in RFC 5618, IANA reserved a new capability named DSCP and ECN Monitoring Capability at bit position 8, with its semantics defined in Section 2 of this RFC.
sections.eli5: The new option got its own numbered switch on the list of options, so nobody else uses that switch for something different.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says DSCP and ECN monitoring does not appear to add any security threat to hosts that communicate with TWAMP as defined in RFC 5357 and its existing extensions such as RFC 6038. The security considerations that apply to any active measurement of live networks are relevant here too, and the Security Considerations sections of RFC 4656 and RFC 5357 apply.
sections.eli5: Writing down the sticker does not give a bad guy anything new to use, but the usual care about measuring real networks still applies.
